To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) Low‐frequency mossy fibres stimulation induces LTD; (2) LTD induction depends on [Ca2+]i; (3) the [Ca2+]‐dependence of LTD induction resembles the BCM rule; (4) the changes in neurotransmission associated with LTD induction are opposite to those characterising LTP.

low‐frequency moss fibre stimulation induces long‐term depression of neurotransmitter release, and this plasticity is associated with an increase of the coefficient of variation, failure rate and paired‐pulse ratio.
low‐frequency stimulation (100 impulses s−1) induces LTD, whereas high‐frequency stimulation (300 impulses s−1 or longer) induces LTP.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the question of how different frequencies and patterns of spike discharges of mossy fibre afferents to cerebellar granule cells induce long‐term plastic changes in neurotransmitter (GABA and glutamate) release.
the question of how the cerebellum processes sensory inputs and how the cerebellar cortex is involved in motor learning.
the mechanisms underlying learning in the cerebellar cortex and the role of the cerebellum for motor learning.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the induction of LTD by mossy fibre activation is a function of the frequency and duration, but not of the total number, of presynaptic action potentials.

the cerebellar mossy fiber-granule cell synapses are able to encode the frequency of mossy fiber input by the induction of bidirectional plasticity, which may be important in the cerebellum for the processing and storage of spatiotemporal information.
the frequency of stimulation of the mossy fibe–granule cell system determines the balance between LTD and LTP, and this effect is mediated by the NMDA receptor.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the cerebellum is a good place to study how the nervous system learns to process information.

frequency‐coded patterns induce bidirectional long‐terminal changes in neurotransmitter releases at the mossy fiber–granule cell (MFG) synapse of the cerebellum, which is the first stage of the cerebellar cortex.
the frequency of mossy fibre stimulation determines whether LTP or LTD is induced.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the frequency of mossy fibre stimulation is a major factor in determining the balance between long‐term potentiations and long‐term depressions at the cerebellum input.
the induction of bidirectional synaptic plasticity by sensory stimulation depends on the frequency and duration, but not on the number, of action potentials.

frequency‐coded patterns of synaptic activity are converted into bidirectional long‐lasting changes of neurotransmitter release by a mechanism that is common to the expression of both long‐term depression and long‐term facilitation.
